sources.title: Preparing Your Older Child for a New Baby: How to Help Siblings Adjust
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 10 Feb 2026)
sources.quote: Expect your child to regress a little. ... your toilet-trained child might suddenly start having 'accidents,' or they might want to take a bottle. ... Plan a one-on-one date with your child. ... Set aside special time for your child. ... Find ways to invite your child to help. ... You want to make sure your child feels included and not excluded. ... Praise them when they are gentle and loving toward the baby. ... Reassure your child that you will love them just as much after the baby is born, as you do now. ... Read children's books about newborns and siblings with your child.
sources.supports: Regression is expected, one-on-one time, inviting the child to help, feeling included, praise for gentleness, reassurance of love, and reading children's books about siblings. AAP parent page, general advice.

sources.title: "When Is He Going Back in Your Belly?" How to Help Older Siblings Adjust to the New Baby
sources.quote: Taking steps backwards in development is often a sign of stress. ... Encouraging or demanding that older children act 'like a big boy or girl' often backfires. ... Encourage your older child to help with the new baby, but don't force it. ... Don't make everything about the new baby.
sources.supports: Regression is often a sign of stress, do not demand 'big kid' behaviour, invite help without forcing it, and keep some focus on the older child.

sources.title: How to Cope With After-School Meltdowns
sources.quote: Going to school can be completely exhausting for many kids. ... Many children come home starving and dehydrated, even if they communicate otherwise. ... Get ahead of the hunger crash by planning the after school snacks in advance. ... Leave the questions for later. ... most kids need time to decompress and zone out before discussing the daily play-by-play. ... A simple greeting and a hug or high-five is a great way to connect and provide emotional space from the school day. ... Many of them lack sufficient time to play, run and regroup throughout the day. ... Let your child speak without attempting to fix any identified problems.
sources.supports: School is tiring, hunger and thirst after school, questions later, time to decompress, a warm greeting, time to play and run, and listening without fixing. Page about school age children in general.

sources.title: Restraint collapse: Why kids fall apart after school
sources.quote: A snack can help your child get back on an even keel. ... Don't ask about negatives first. ... the need to share or connect about their day
sources.supports: A snack first, do not open with negative questions, and connect about the day before demands such as homework or chores. General advice for school age children, not specific to first grade.

sources.title: How to Cope With After-School Meltdowns
sources.quote: Going to school can be completely exhausting for many kids. ... Many children come home starving and dehydrated, even if they communicate otherwise. ... Get ahead of the hunger crash by planning the after school snacks in advance. ... Leave the questions for later. ... most kids need time to decompress and zone out before discussing the daily play-by-play. ... A simple greeting and a hug or high-five is a great way to connect and provide emotional space from the school day. ... Many of them lack sufficient time to play, run and regroup throughout the day. ... Let your child speak without attempting to fix any identified problems.
sources.supports: School is tiring, hunger and thirst after school, questions later, time to decompress, a warm greeting, time to play and run, and listening without fixing. Page about school age children in general.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one way Zero To Three suggests to help a child with feelings. The page is about empathy, not about school; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment.
